# 20 - Prior Hospitalization and Transfer Requirements

(Rev. 1, 10-01-03)

A3-3131, SNF-212

In order to qualify for post-hospital extended care services, the individual must have been an inpatient of a hospital for a medically necessary stay of at least three consecutive calendar days. In addition, effective December 5, 1980, the individual must have been transferred to a participating SNF within 30 days after discharge from the hospital, unless the exception in §20.2 applies.

## 20.1 - Three-Day Prior Hospitalization

(Rev. 10880, Issued: 08-06-21, Effective: 11-08-21, Implementation: 11-08-21)

In accordance with section 226(c)(1)(B) of the Social Security Act and the implementing regulations at 42 CFR 409.30(a)(2), the hospital discharge must have occurred on or after the first day of the month in which the individual attained age 65 or, effective July 1, 1973, became entitled to health insurance benefits under the disability or chronic renal disease provisions of the law. The 3 consecutive calendar day stay requirement can be met by stays totaling 3 consecutive days in one or more hospitals. In determining whether the requirement has been met, the day of admission, but not the day of discharge, is counted as a hospital inpatient day.

Time spent in observation or in the emergency room prior to (or in lieu of) an inpatient admission to the hospital does not count toward the 3-day qualifying inpatient hospital stay, as a person who appears at a hospital’s emergency room seeking examination or treatment or is placed on observation has not been admitted to the hospital as an inpatient; instead, the person receives outpatient services. For purposes of the SNF benefit’s qualifying hospital stay requirement, inpatient status commences with the calendar day of hospital admission. See 31 Fed. Reg. 10116, 10118-19 (July 27, 1966).

To be covered, the extended care services must have been for the treatment of a condition for which the beneficiary was receiving inpatient hospital services (including services of an emergency hospital) or a condition which arose while in the SNF for treatment of a condition for which the beneficiary was previously hospitalized. In this context, the applicable hospital condition need not have been the principal diagnosis that actually precipitated the beneficiary’s admission to the hospital, but could be any one of the conditions present during the qualifying hospital stay.

In addition, the qualifying hospital stay must have been medically necessary. Medical necessity will generally be presumed to exist. When the facts that come to the A/B MACs (A) attention during the course of its normal claims review process indicate that the hospitalization may not have been medically necessary, it will fully develop the case, checking with the attending physician and the hospital, as appropriate. The A/B MAC will rule the stay unnecessary only when hospitalization for 3 days represents a substantial departure from normal medical practice. However, in accordance with Pub. 100-04, Medicare Claims Processing Manual, Chapter 30, §130.2.A, when a beneficiary qualifies for limitation on liability in connection with the hospital stay (or a portion thereof), this conclusively establishes that the hospital stay (or portion thereof) was not medically necessary.

Even if a beneficiary’s care during a qualifying hospital stay becomes less intensive during the latter part of the stay, the date of hospital “discharge” in this context is still considered to be the day that the beneficiary physically leaves the hospital, and the level of care being furnished at that particular point is not a determining factor as long as some portion of the stay included at least 3 consecutive days of medically necessary inpatient hospital services. In addition, when a hospital inpatient’s care needs drop from acute- to SNF-level but no SNF bed is available, the regulations at 42 CFR 424.13(c) permit a physician to certify that the beneficiary’s continued inpatient stay in the hospital is, in fact, medically necessary under this particular set of circumstances (see also Pub. 100-01, Medicare General Information, Eligibility, and Entitlement Manual, Chapter 4, §10.6). Accordingly, such additional, “alternate placement” days spent in the hospital can be included in the 3-day count toward meeting the SNF benefit’s qualifying hospital stay requirement.

The 3-day hospital stay need not be in a hospital with which the SNF has a transfer agreement (see Pub. 100-01, Medicare General Information, Eligibility, and Entitlement Manual, Chapter 5, §30.2 for a discussion of the SNF’s required transfer agreement with a hospital). However, the hospital must be either a Medicare-participating hospital or an institution that meets at least the conditions of participation for an emergency services hospital (see Pub. 100-01, Medicare General Information, Eligibility, and Entitlement Manual, Chapter 5, §20.2, for the definition of an emergency services hospital). A nonparticipating psychiatric hospital need not meet the special requirements applicable to psychiatric hospitals (see Pub. 100-01, Medicare General Information, Eligibility, and Entitlement Manual, Chapter 5, §20.3). Stays in Religious Nonmedical Health Care Institutions (see Pub. 100-01, Medicare General Information, Eligibility, and Entitlement Manual, Chapter 5, §40, for definition of RNHCIs) are excluded for the purpose of satisfying the 3-day period of hospitalization. See Pub. 100-02, Medicare Benefit Policy Manual, Chapter 9, §40.1.5, regarding a qualifying stay that consists of “general inpatient care” furnished in a hospital under the hospice benefit.

NOTE: While a 3-day stay in a psychiatric hospital satisfies the prior hospital stay requirement, institutions that primarily provide psychiatric treatment cannot participate in the program as SNFs. Therefore, a patient with only a psychiatric condition who is transferred from a psychiatric hospital to a participating SNF is likely to receive only non-covered care. In the SNF setting, the term “non-covered care” refers to any level of care less intensive than the SNF level of care that is covered under the program. (See §§30ff.).

# Section 20: The Hospital Stay Your Parent Needs Before Medicare Pays for Nursing Home Care

*(Revision 1, October 1, 2003. Old references: A3-3131, SNF-212.)*

A skilled nursing facility (SNF) is a nursing home that gives daily nursing or therapy care. Medicare Part A can pay for a short SNF stay after a hospital stay. Two rules must be met first.

1. **The hospital stay rule.** Your parent must have been a hospital inpatient for at least 3 days in a row. The stay must have been medically needed.
2. **The 30-day rule.** Your parent must move to the SNF within 30 days of leaving the hospital. The SNF must take part in Medicare. This rule has applied since December 5, 1980. There is one exception, described in Section 20.2.

## 20.1: The 3-Day Hospital Stay

*(Revision 10880. Issued August 6, 2021. Effective November 8, 2021.)*

### When the hospital stay must happen

The hospital discharge must happen on or after a certain date. That date is the first day of the month when your parent:

- turned 65, or
- became eligible for Medicare because of a disability or kidney failure. (This option began July 1, 1973.)

This comes from section 226(c)(1)(B) of the Social Security Act. It also comes from federal rule 42 CFR 409.30(a)(2).

### How the days are counted

- The 3 days must be in a row.
- The days can be spread across more than one hospital.
- The day your parent is admitted counts.
- The day your parent leaves does **not** count.

**Example:** Your parent is admitted Monday and leaves Thursday. Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday count. That is 3 days, so the rule is met.

### Observation and emergency room time do not count

An "inpatient" is a person the hospital has formally admitted. Some patients stay in the hospital without being admitted. This can happen in two ways:

- **Emergency room (ER) time.** Your parent is seen or treated in the ER.
- **Observation.** Observation means the hospital watches your parent to decide whether to admit them.

In both cases your parent is an "outpatient." An outpatient is someone who gets hospital care without being admitted. This is true even if they stay overnight. Outpatient time does not count toward the 3 days.

The count starts on the day your parent is formally admitted as an inpatient.

**Tip:** Ask the hospital staff whether your parent is "inpatient" or "under observation." Ask more than once during the stay.

### The SNF care must relate to the hospital stay

Medicare pays for SNF care only if it treats one of these:

- a condition your parent was treated for in the hospital, or
- a new condition that started in the SNF while they were being treated there for the hospital condition.

The condition does not have to be the main reason your parent went to the hospital. It can be any condition they had during the hospital stay.

### The hospital stay must have been medically needed

Medicare usually assumes the hospital stay was needed.

Sometimes a claim raises doubts. Then the Medicare Administrative Contractor (MAC) looks into it. A MAC is the company that handles Medicare claims in your parent's area. The MAC may talk with your parent's doctor and the hospital.

The MAC will say the stay was not needed only in one case. That case is when a 3-day stay is far outside normal medical practice.

There is one more case to know about. Sometimes Medicare protects a patient from paying for care that turned out not to be covered. This protection is called "limitation on liability." It applies when the patient could not have known the care would not be covered. If your parent got this protection for any part of the hospital stay, that part counts as not medically needed. That part then cannot count toward the 3 days. (See the Medicare Claims Processing Manual, Chapter 30, Section 130.2.A.)

### Lighter care near the end of the stay

Your parent's care may become less intense near the end of the hospital stay. That is fine. The discharge date is the day your parent physically leaves the hospital. The rule is met if at least 3 days in a row were medically needed inpatient care.

### Waiting in the hospital for a nursing home bed

Sometimes a patient no longer needs hospital-level care. They now need nursing-home-level care. But no SNF bed is open yet.

In this case, a doctor can state in writing that staying in the hospital is medically needed. The days spent waiting are called "alternate placement" days. These days **do** count toward the 3 days. (See federal rule 42 CFR 424.13(c). Also see the Medicare General Information, Eligibility, and Entitlement Manual, Chapter 4, Section 10.6.)

### Which hospitals count

- The hospital does **not** need a special transfer agreement with the SNF.
- The hospital **must** take part in Medicare. Or it must meet Medicare's standards for an emergency services hospital.
- A psychiatric hospital does not need to take part in Medicare. It also does not need to meet Medicare's extra rules for psychiatric hospitals.
- Stays in a Religious Nonmedical Health Care Institution (RNHCI) do **not** count. An RNHCI gives care based on religious beliefs instead of medical treatment.
- A stay can also count if your parent was on hospice and got inpatient hospital care through hospice. Hospice is comfort care for people near the end of life. See the Medicare Benefit Policy Manual, Chapter 9, Section 40.1.5.

These sources have more detail: the Medicare General Information, Eligibility, and Entitlement Manual, Chapter 5, Sections 20.2, 20.3, 30.2 and 40.

### Note on psychiatric hospital stays

A 3-day stay in a psychiatric hospital does meet the hospital stay rule. But a facility that mainly gives psychiatric care cannot be a Medicare SNF.

So a patient may have only a mental health condition. If that patient moves from a psychiatric hospital to an SNF, Medicare will likely not pay for the SNF care.

"Non-covered care" means care that is less than the skilled level Medicare pays for. Section 30 and the sections after it explain this more.
